newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa eases fx controls on individuals, firms.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa eases fx controls on individuals, firms.

text.p: Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Wednesday announced the next steps in the relaxation of South African exchange controls, focusing this time on individuals and corporates.

Individuals will be allowed to invest a limited amount of capital overseas or hold foreign currency bank accounts from July 1, while South African companies would also gain the freedom to transact internationally.
At the same time there will be some amendments to widen the options for institutional investors who have had the right to invest offshore using asset swaps since July 1995.
"I believe that the conditions are now right for a significant instalment in the relaxation of exchange controls," Manuel said in his budget speech.

A joint statement from Manuel and Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals said the balance of payments position and the involvement of the central bank in the forward market made it impossible to allow unlimited capital transfers at present.
But the package of measures, most of which take effect from July 1, would move South Africa to a system with a positive rather than a negative bias with regard to capital movement.
Key elements of the package are as follows:

- individuals will be allowed to invest a limited amount of capital overseas or alternatively maintain foreign currency deposit accounts with South African banks subject to a prescribed ceiling which will be announced before July;
- individuals will be allowed to retain foreign income earnings in foreign currency accounts;
- individuals will be able to remit an amount of capital abroad, with extended limits for buying fixed property in Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries;
- South African corporations will be allowed to raise foreign funding on the strength of their South African balance sheet;
- South African companies establishing new ventures will be allowed to transfer up to 30 million rand as a proportion of their investment, or 40 million in SADC states;

- the time limit within which foreign exchange must be sold to authorised dealers will rise to 30 days from seven and the threshold below which documents are required for the purchase or sale of foreign exchange will increase to 40,000 rand from 2,000;
- corporates will be free to invest an as yet undecided percentage of their assets abroad (based on audited balance sheets) for portfolio investments, "when circumstances permit";

- institutions will again to be allowed to make foreign acquisitions during 1997 of up to three percent of the net inflow of funds last year, as in 1996, with a further two percent for the purchase of stock listed on SADC exchanges;

- the 10 percent limit applicable to acquisition of foreign portfolio assets will apply to all the assets under management in any specific unit trust scheme, and the definition of qualifying institutions for asset swaps will be widened to include regulated fund managers;

- the development of a dollar-rand futures contract on the South African Futures Exchange (Safex) will be backed by the Reserve Bank, with participation initialy limited to non-residents and authorised foreign exchange dealers;
- the non-resident ownership level at which foreign controlled entities become subject to limits on local borrowing will be raised from 25 to 50 percent;
- non-residents will be allowed to maintain foreign currency accounts with South African banks;
- most remaining controls on current account transactions will be abolished;
- travel allowances are increased to 80,000 rand a year per adult and 25,000 per child.
"The changes in the exchange control regime announced here are profound," Manuel said.

"We move now to an environment in which South Africans can make ordinary transactions abroad freely, while the constraints which remain on large movements of capital will increasingly give way to procedural and prudential supervision."
